section: Descriptive Statistics for the Entire Sample
text:
Descriptive Statistics for the Entire Sample
Using the Climate Change Trust Scale (Barchard, Hoffman, Okagawa, & Odents, 2021), we asked participants to tell us how much they trusted politicians and scientists, with response options 1 = None at all, 2 = A little, 3 = Moderate, 4 = A lot, 5 = A great deal. You will determine who participants trust more.

Under the Exploration menu, click Descriptives.



Calculate descriptive statistics for the variable CCTS_Politicians_Say (“How much do you trust what politicians say about climate change?”) and variable CCTS_Scientists_Say (“How much do you trust what scientists say about climate change?”).
Ask it to calculate three statistics that measure Central Tendency: Mean, Median, and Mode.
Ask it to calculate three statistics that measure Dispersion: Standard Deviation, Variance, and Range.


Check your answers

title: Descriptive Statistics in jamovi
text:
Descriptive Statistics for Subsamples
Often researchers are interested in particular groups of participants. Here, we will calculate trust separately for people who identify as female, male, and non-binary.

To create another analysis without erasing the old one, click Exploration, then Descriptives.
Calculate descriptive statistics for the same two variables: CCTS_Politicians_Say (“How much do you trust what politicians say about climate change?”) and variable CCTS_Scientists_Say (“How much do you trust what scientists say about climate change?”). However, this time, split the results by Gender.
Calculate the same six statistics as last time: mean, median, mode, standard deviation, variance, and range.

title: Subgroups in jamovi
text:
Splitting the Data
We want to know whether belief in climate change is influenced by personal experience. To determine this, we asked all participants to indicate if they believe the world’s climate is changing (with response options yes, no, and don’t know) and to rate how much they agreed with the statement “I have been directly affected by climate change” on a five-point frequency scale (with response options 1 = Never,2 = Rarely, 3 = Sometimes, 4 = Often, and 5 = Almost always). This second question is Item 14 on the Psychological Responses to Climate Change Climate Change (Clayton & Karazsia, 2020).

Calculate sample size (N), mean, median, and mode for the variable PRCC14 (“I have been directly affected by climate change”)
Split the file by Doubt1 (“As far as you know, do you personally think that the world’s climate is changing?”) to obtain separate results for the three groups: yes, no, and don’t know.
Add histograms so you can better visualize your data.
Use the results to answer the questions below.

Filtering 1
Like splitting data, filters can be used to get separate results for groups that are labelled by categorical variables, but filters can also be used to explore the effect of continuous variables.

Under the Data tab, click Filters.
To view only participants who responded that they believe the world’s climate is changing, add the filter: Doubt1 == ’Yes’. Note the capital Y on “Yes”.
Jamovi applies this filter to ALL of the results in your output window. To see this, look at your histogram. Now that the filter for Doubt1 is active, answer Question 3 below.

title: Introduction to jamovi
text:
The purpose of this exercise is to introduce you to jamovi, a powerful, easy-to-use statistics program that is also FREE. You can install jamovi on your Windows, Mac, Linux, or Chromebook. If you do not have access to one of those types of computers, you can use jamovi in a simple online format. In this exercise, you will learn the basics of jamovi and then use it to calculate some probabilities.
During this exercise, you will explore probabilities related to sustainability. If you want to learn more about sustainability and climate change, see What You Can do About Climate Change.

title: Introduction to jamovi
text:
Calculate Simple Probabilities
Calculate the percentage of participants who often wish or almost always wish they behaved more sustainably. To do this:

Click the Frequencies menu.
In the Contingency Tables section, click Independent Samples.
Move the variable PRCC17 (“I wish I behaved more sustainably.”) to Rows. To do this, highlight the variable PRCC17. Then click the arrow that points to the right to move this variable into the box that says Rows.
Move Gender to Columns.
Look at the right-hand side of jamovi, where it shows your output. You should see a Contingency Table with four columns and six rows.


Columns are vertical. You should have columns for Female, Male, Non-binary, and Total.
Rows are horizontal. You should have rows for Never, Rarely, Sometimes, Often, Almost always, and Total.
Cells are the intersections of rows and columns. There should be 24 cells in your table; each cell should have a number in it.


Look at the left-hand side of jamovi, again, where you tell it what analysis you want to do. In the Cells section, check the box to indicate you want the Percentages for Row.
In the output table, look at the row that says Total. Read off the percentage of participants who are male.


Note that jamovi considers percentages to be 2 decimals. For example, 32% is 2 decimals, whereas 32.78% would be 4 decimals. In this course, we will present results to 2 decimals.







TipQuestion 1



What percentage of participants are male (whole number)? 



In jamovi, in the Cells section, indicate you want the Percentages for Column. To make the output easier to read, uncheck the box that shows the Percentages for Row.
In the output table, look at the column that says Total.


22% of participants said they often wish they behaved more sustainably.
Find the percentage who said they almost always wish they behaved more sustainably.
Add these percentages together.







TipQuestion 2



What percentage of participants often or almost always wish they behaved more sustainably (whole number)?

Calculate a Joint Probability
A joint probability is the probability of two events occurring simultaneously. Calculate the percentage of participants who are female and who rarely wish they behaved more sustainably. To do this:

In the Cells section, indicate you want the Percentages for Total. To make your output easier to read, you can uncheck the box for Column.
On your output table, look in the cell for female and rarely. Read off the percentage of participants who are female and rarely wish they behaved more sustainably.







TipQuestion 3



What percentage of female participants rarely wish they behaved more sustainably (whole number)?

title: Introduction to jamovi
text:
Calculate a Conditional Probability

A conditional probability is the probability of one event occurring assuming another event has already occurred. For those people who almost always wish they behaved more sustainably, calculate the percentage who are female. To do this:
In the Cells section, indicate you want percentages for Row.To make your output easier to read, you can uncheck the box for Total.
Look at the row of results for almost always. Of participants who almost always wish they behaved more sustainably, read the percentage who are female.







TipQuestion 4

title: Transforming data in jamovi
text:
Creating a grouping variable
When participants completed our study, they told us their age. We used that information to divide participants into two groups: under 30 and over 30. Here, you will learn how that is done. You will create a new transformed variable that assigns participants to two groups based upon their numeric answers for the variable Age. To do this:

Insert a New Transformed Variable next to the current Age variable. To insert the variable, click the Data menu and click on the variable Age. Click Add. In the drop-down menu, using Transformed Variable, click Insert.
Create a New Transform named “Grouping by Age”. To create this transform, click “using transform.” Click Create New Transform.
In the description, explain what the transform does in more detail: “Recodes age into two categories”
Under variable suffix, type “2 Groups”.
Add recode conditions:


if $source > 29 use “30+”
else use “Under 30”


Under Measure type, select Nominal. Then close the New Transform dialogue.




Recode age into two categories using the Transform dialogue

title: Transforming data in jamovi
text:
Reverse-Coding an Item
Eleven of the variables in this data set were designed to measure hope about climate change (Li & Monroe, 2017). They are:

I believe people will be able to solve problems caused by climate change. (CCHS1)
I believe scientists will be able to find ways to solve problems caused by climate change. (CCHS2)
Even when some people give up, I know there will be others who will continue to try to solve problems caused by climate change. (CCHS3)
If everyone works together, we can solve problems caused by climate change. (CCHS4)
I am willing to take actions to help solve problems caused by climate change. (CCHS5)
I believe more people are willing to take actions to help solve problems caused by climate change.(CCHS6)
I know that there are things that I can do to help solve problems caused by climate change. (CCHS7)
I know what to do to help solve problems caused by climate change. (CCHS8)
Climate change is beyond my control, so I won’t even bother trying to solve problems caused by climate change. (CCHS9)
Climate change is so complex we will not be able to solve problems that it causes. (CCHS10)
The actions I can take are too small to help solve problems caused by climate change. (CCHS11)

For most of these items, higher scores indicate more hope. However, for three of the variables, higher scores indicate less hope. These variables are CCHS9 (“Climate change is beyond my control, so I won’t even bother trying to solve problems caused by climate change.”), CCHS10 (“Climate change is so complex we will not be able to solve problems that it causes.”) and CCHS11 (“The actions I can take are too small to help solve problems caused by climate change.”). We need to reverse code those three variables. To do this:

Create a New Transformed Variable at the end of the data set.
Create a New Transform called “Reverse Coding”. Use the suffix “R”. Provide an appropriate description for this transform.
Add seven recode conditions:


if $source == 1 use 7
if $source == 2 use 6
if $source == 3 use 5
if $source == 4 use 4
if $source == 5 use 3
if $source == 6 use 2
if $source == 7 use 1


To indicate missing responses, use


else use NA


Under Measure type, select Continuous.
Apply the Reverse Coding transform to the variables CCHS9, CCHS10 and CCHS11 to create variables CCHS9 - R, CCHS10 - R, and CCHS11 - R. Provide appropriate descriptions for the three new variables.




Calculate the means for CCHS9, CCHS10, CCHS11, CCHS9 - R, CCHS10 - R, and CCHS11 - R.
If you did your reverse coding correctly, your means should match those in the table below.
If the mean for CCHS9, CCHS10 or CCHS11 is incorrect, there’s something wrong with your data set. Download the data set from the OSF website again, and then re-do this assignment.
If the mean for CCHS9 - R, CCHS10 - R or CCHS11 - R is incorrect, there’s something wrong with your reverse coding. Edit your transformation and fix the error(s).

section: Compute a Total Score for the Climate Change Hope Scale
text:
Compute a Total Score for the Climate Change Hope Scale
Compute total scores for the Climate Change Hope Scale (Li & Monroe, 2017) using the recoded variables you created in the previous section. To do this:

Create a New Computed Variable named “CCHS”.
Under description, type “Total score for Climate Change Hope Scale”.
In the functions drop-down menu, double-click the statistical function SUM to add it to your formula.
Double-click on the variable CCHS1 to add it to your formula. Then type a comma.
Double-click on each of the remaining variables to add them one by one into the function. Separate them with commas. Your final function should read:

SUM (`CCHS1`, `CCHS2`, `CCHS3`, `CCHS4`, `CCHS5`, `CCHS6`, `CCHS7`, `CCHS8`, `CCHS9 - R`, `CCHS10 - R`, `CCHS11 - R`)


Double check that you have a total of 11 variables and that you used the recoded variables CCHS9 - R, CCHS10 - R and CCHS11 - R.
You should now have the total scores for your new variable CCHS. Calculate the mean for CCHS.
Use this mean to answer Question 2.







TipQuestion 2



The mean for the CCHS is  (2dp).



Split the results by Age – Categorical.
Use these results to answer Question 3.

title: Transforming data in jamovi
text:
Recoding Missing Values
Jamovi ignores missing values when running analyses. This can lead to erroneous conclusions. For example, participants were asked how frequently they eat vegetarian/vegan meals. The possible response options were
1 = Less than once a year
2 = Once a year
3 = Several times a year
4 = Once a month
5 = A couple times a month
6 = Once a week
7 = At least 3 times a week
8 = At least 7 times a week
9 = At least 14 times a week
Participants who did not answer this question probably eat vegetarian/vegan meals less than once a year. Therefore, we need to recode any missing values for the CCAI_Food3 variable to 1 (less than once a year) in order to get accurate means for this question. To do this:

Create a new transform. Name it “Missing Values”.
Add an accurate description of what the transformation is doing (e.g., “Recodes system missing values to 1”.)
Use the variable suffix “MissingTo1”.
Add a recode condition that says

if $source == NA use 1

To keep the other values the same, use

else use $source

Under Measure type, select Continuous.
Use this new transform to recode the variable CCAI_Food3.
Add an appropriate description for this variable (e.g., “CCAI_Food3 with missing values recoded to 1”).




Calculate total number of responses (N), number of missing values, and mean for the original variable (CCAI_Food3) and for the transformed variable (e.g., CCAI_Food3 – MissingTo1).
Split the above results by Age – Categorical to find out how often participants who are under 30 or 30+ eat vegetarian/vegan meals.
Use these results to answer the questions below. Who eats more vegetarian/vegan meals - under-30s or 30+ folks?







TipQuestion 4



Once you recode missing values to 1, the mean for vegetarian/vegan meals eaten by under-30s is  (2dp).








TipQuestion 5



Once you recode missing values to 1, the mean for vegetarian/vegan meals eaten by over-30s is  (2dp).

title: Transforming data in jamovi
text:
Check Your Work

Your jamovi file should include the data set with the six new variables: Age – 2 Groups, CCHS9 - R, CCHS10 - R, CCHS11 - R, CCHS, and CCAI_Food3 - MissingTo1.
Your jamovi output should include:


means for CCHS9, CCHS10, CCHS11, CCHS9 - R, CCHS10 - R, and CCHS11 – R,
the mean score on the Climate Change Hope Scale for participants who are under 30 and 30+, and
the mean frequency of vegetarian/vegan meals eaten for participants who are under 30 and 30+, both for the original variables and for the transformed variable.


Save your data file with an appropriate name so you can find it later.
